content.title: About
content.content: Beef with mushroom sauce is a dish made from premium cuts of beef, seared to a golden crust and simmered in a fragrant sauce of mushrooms, cream, and spices. The sauce gives the dish a smooth, creamy flavor with a subtle mushroom note.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is a rich source of iron that is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.
Button mushrooms are one of the most widely cultivated edible mushrooms worldwide.
Traditionally, beef with mushroom sauce is served in French and Italian restaurants.
Cream in the sauce adds richness and helps retain the aromatic compounds of the mushrooms.
The dish is quick to prepare: searing the beef takes 5‑7 minutes, and simmering in the sauce adds another 15‑20 minutes.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support the immune system and normal nerve function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef is rich in B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Mushrooms – source of vitamin D
items.content: Button mushrooms, especially when exposed to UV light, contain vitamin D, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Cream – source of vitamin A and fat‑soluble vitamins
items.content: Cream adds vitamin A and aids the absorption of other fat‑soluble vitamins in the dish.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Cream and certain cuts of beef can raise saturated fat intake, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cream may trigger reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Using prepared broths or soy sauces can increase the dish’s salt content.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Beef should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C to prevent salmonella and other bacterial infections.

content.title: How to Serve
content.content: Serve the dish hot, garnished with fresh herbs such as parsley or dill. It pairs well with mashed potatoes, rice, pasta, or a fresh vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftover beef with mushroom sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze for 2‑3 months. Reheat thoroughly to a rolling boil before serving to ensure safety.

content.title: About
content.content: Haupia is a traditional Hawaiian dessert made from coconut milk thickened with starch (usually corn starch). It has a delicate creamy coconut flavor, a light jelly‑like texture, and is typically served chilled.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Hawaiian word “haupia,” which simply means “coconut dessert.”
Traditionally the dessert was set in large wooden bowls and then cut into cubes.
In the United States haupia is often used as a filling for cakes, pastries, and ice cream.
Coconut milk, the main ingredient, is rich in lauric acid, giving it a distinctive aroma.
Haupia can be made gluten‑free by using tapioca or potato starch instead of wheat‑based thickeners.

items.title: Rich in medium‑chain triglycerides
items.content: Coconut milk contains MCTs that may support quick energy and metabolism.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: In modest amounts, coconut milk provides vitamin C, which helps the immune system.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and muscle function.

items.title: Gluten‑ and lactose‑free
items.content: Haupia is suitable for people with celiac disease or lactose intolerance.

items.title: Low sugar when prepared accordingly
items.content: If only a small amount of sugar or a sugar substitute is used, the dessert remains moderately sweet.

items.title: Coconut allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut milk.

items.title: High in saturated fat
items.content: Coconut milk is high in saturated fat, so people with elevated cholesterol should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: The dessert can be calorie‑dense, especially when sweetened.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Traditional recipes often call for a generous amount of sugar, which may be problematic for diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve haupia chilled, cut into cubes or slices. It can be enjoyed on its own, used as a filling for cakes, pastries, ice cream, or incorporated into cocktails and fruit salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep prepared haupia in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size containers for up to 2 months. Before serving, allow it to fully thaw and chill slightly.

content.title: About
content.content: Kidney beans are large, kidney‑shaped legumes known for their deep red color. In canned form they are fully cooked and ready to eat, and the reduced‑sodium version (2151 mg/100 g) makes them suitable for low‑salt diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the bean’s shape, which resembles a human kidney.
Red beans contain anthocyanins that give them their vivid color.
Canning preserves most of the bean’s nutrients, including protein and fiber.
They are a staple in Mexican, Creole, and South American cuisines.
Reduced‑sodium cans achieve lower salt levels by substituting part of the salt with flavorful spices.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: A typical serving (about 130 g) provides roughly 8 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps keep you feeling full.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are essential for blood formation and preventing anemia.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: Reduced salt makes this product a good choice for people monitoring blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in kidney beans help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Raw toxicity
items.content: Uncooked kidney beans contain phytohaemagglutinin, a toxic protein. Canning destroys it, but raw beans must never be eaten.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Legumes can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals; introduce them gradually.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some people may experience an allergic reaction to beans.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While nutritious, beans are relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned kidney beans can be tossed into salads, soups, chili, stews, and pasta dishes. They are ready to use straight from the can—simply drain the liquid, optionally rinse, and add. For a milder flavor, rinse briefly with cold water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place. After opening, transfer beans to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for up to 3–4 days. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: A milk shake is a cold beverage made from milk, cream and various flavorings, commonly served in fast‑food restaurants. Non‑chocolate versions include vanilla, strawberry, banana, caramel and nut flavors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first milk shake appeared in the United States in the early 20th century as a "milk frappe".
In Russia the milk shake became popular in the 1990s alongside the expansion of fast‑food chains.
Non‑chocolate shakes often use real fruit purées, increasing their vitamin content.
There are "shake bars" where customers can mix several flavors into one drink.
Traditionally the shake is served in a tall glass with a straw, sometimes topped with whipped cream and sprinkles.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Milk, the main ingredient, is rich in calcium, which supports bone and teeth health.

items.title: Protein rich
items.content: Cream and milk provide complete protein that aids muscle repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk shakes contain vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotics (when yogurt is added)
items.content: If yogurt is used, the shake can help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Antioxidants (with fruit flavors)
items.content: Fruit additions like strawberry or blueberry supply vitamin C and polyphenols.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance should use lactose‑free milk or plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Sweet syrups and flavorings can raise calorie count and blood glucose levels.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Some flavors (e.g., nut) contain nuts and may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Excess calories
items.content: Large portions can contribute to weight gain if consumed frequently.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The shake is served cold, typically in a 300–500 ml glass. It is drunk through a straw and can also be used as a topping for pancakes, waffles or ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Prepared shake should be kept in the refrigerator for no more than 2 hours. If components (milk, cream, fruit purée) are pre‑made, store them in sealed containers for up to 24 hours.

content.title: About
content.content: Sprouts, NFS (4524) are fresh sprouts grown using a natural, hormone‑free method (NFS – Natural Fresh Sprouts). The sprouts are rich in vitamins, minerals and enzymes, have a crunchy texture and a mild, slightly nutty flavor. They are used in salads, smoothies, sandwiches, or enjoyed as a healthy snack on their own.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sprouts can be grown from a variety of seeds: wheat, peas, soy, beans and more.
Because of their short growth cycle (3–7 days) they retain maximum nutrients.
Sprouts contain more vitamin C than most mature vegetables.
The NFS method excludes chemical growth stimulants and pesticides.
Sprouts have been used in traditional Asian cuisine for over a thousand years.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Sprouts provide vitamins B1, B2, B3 and folate, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: They contain polyphenols and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: High dietary fiber and enzymes promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Sprouts are low in calories, making them an excellent choice for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Contains essential minerals
items.content: Sprouts supply iron, magnesium, zinc and potassium, important for overall body function.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Raw sprouts can harbor Salmonella or E. coli; keep them refrigerated and wash thoroughly before eating.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to specific seed varieties used for sprouting.

items.title: Not recommended for young children
items.content: Due to choking hazards, avoid giving small sprouts to children under 5 years old.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add sprouts to salads, soups, sandwiches, smoothies, or eat them as a standalone snack. Before consumption, rinse them under running water and, if desired, briefly blanch in hot water to reduce microbial load.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sprouts in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1–4 °C. Use them within 3–5 days. Discard if they develop an off‑odor or a slimy film.
